verses.text: This is the third time I am coming to you. “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.”

I have said beforehand, and I do say beforehand, as when I was present the second time, so now, being absent, I write to those who have sinned before now, and to all the rest, that, if I come again, I will not spare;
seeing that you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me; who toward you is not weak, but is powerful in you.
For he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we will live with him through the power of God toward you.
Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves. Or don’t you know as to your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you? — unless indeed you are disqualified.
But I hope that you will know that we aren’t disqualified.
Now I pray to God that you do no evil; not that we may appear approved, but that you may do that which is honorable, though we are as reprobate.
For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.
For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. And this we also pray for, even your perfecting.
For this cause I write these things while absent, that I may not deal sharply when present, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for building up, and not for tearing down.
Finally, brothers, rejoice. Be perfected, be comforted, be of the same mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you.
Greet one another with a holy kiss.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, God’s love, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. Amen.

footnotes.content: Paul invokes the ancient law: 'At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.' He's warning seriously now—the third visit is coming, and what he hears about them will need witnesses, will matter. God has always bound Himself to truth spoken plainly and testified.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's a tenderness here under the sternness—he's told them beforehand, twice, to warn them. When he returns, he means what he says about not sparing those who've sinned. His delay isn't neglect; it's patience giving room for repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They're testing Paul to prove Christ is really in him. But Paul won't be bullied into performing miracles to satisfy their doubt. Christ speaks through weakness as truly as through power—that's the heart they need to learn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The scandal of the cross itself: Christ was crucified in weakness, yet rose in God's power. Paul is saying we share that pattern—we stumble, we fail, yet Christ lives in us through the same power. Don't mistake weakness for abandonment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He turns the test back on them: examine yourselves. Is Jesus Christ in you? That's the real proof Paul's looking for. Not miracles, not credentials—just the quiet living presence of Jesus already bearing witness in their own hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul isn't worried about being 'disqualified'—his standing rests in Christ, not in their approval. He hopes they'll know that, hope it settles in them like a stone in water. Real authority is never nervous about what people think.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What a prayer: that they do no evil. Not that he'll look good when he arrives. He's willing to appear as reprobate—foolish, disqualified—if it means they walk straight. That's love: wanting their good more than your reputation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A clear compass: we can do nothing against the truth. Every word, every act, every choice must bow to what's true. Paul isn't clever or crafty—he's simply aligned with the truth, and truth can't be bent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He rejoices in his own weakness if it means they grow strong. That's the paradox Paul has learned: when we're broken, Christ's strength shows. He's not praying to be vindicated; he's praying for their maturity—their perfecting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Writing now, from a distance, so he can come in gentleness instead of harshness. The authority Christ gave him is for building up, not tearing down. Every parent knows that difference—correction that restores, not correction that wounds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The final word before blessing: rejoice, be at peace, be of one mind. He's calling them to straightness and wholeness, to living as Jesus taught. The God of love and peace promises His presence when they do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The holy kiss—a sign of peace among brothers and sisters in the early church. Not distant, not cold. Real belonging, real welcome, real reconciliation. Paul is asking them to greet each other in a way that heals.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The saints send their greetings. They are the cloud of witnesses Paul spoke of at the start. You're not alone in this—the whole family of faith stands with you, sending their peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this ancient benediction—grace, love, fellowship, offered to all. Readers today find themselves held by the same Trinity Paul blessed: Jesus makes us righteous, God loves us without measure, the Spirit knits us together. As of 2026-10, His grace and peace remain unchanged.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
